image.subject: Adolph Knigge, a German baron in his thirties, well-fed, embroidered dark-green court coat, powdered hair, a lace jabot, seated at a candle-lit wooden desk in a 1782 study

storyboard.claim: Knigge, code name Philo, is the man who plans the order in 1782.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Knigge at his desk with a quill and the plan on parchment.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the next actor after the flat network of Weishaupt.
storyboard.addedInformation: Knigge's code name is Philo.

image.subject: Adolph Knigge, a German baron in his thirties, well-fed, embroidered dark-green court coat, powdered hair, a lace jabot, bent over a parchment and scratching with a quill

storyboard.claim: Knigge is drafting a new plan for the order by hand.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Knigge writing furiously, quill on parchment.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same man as beat 120, now at work on the document.
storyboard.addedInformation: The plan rewrites the order's structure.

image.subject: a close view of a handwritten parchment page on a wooden desk, its lines struck through with heavy quill strokes beside a guttering candle

storyboard.claim: Knigge deliberately crosses out Weishaupt's egalitarian ideals.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Struck-through lines on a manuscript page.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the destruction described in the prior beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: The deletion is literal, on the page.

storyboard.claim: Weishaupt wanted a network of absolute equals with no ranks.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets up the egalitarian ideal being destroyed.
storyboard.addedInformation: Weishaupt's ideal was utopian.

storyboard.claim: Knigge judged a flat structure a recipe for irrelevance.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns from the ideal to Knigge's verdict on it.
storyboard.addedInformation: A flat network would not matter to anyone.

storyboard.claim: Knigge wrote highly stratified, fake ranks.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the verdict to the solution.
storyboard.addedInformation: The ranks were invented, not inherited.

image.subject: a candle-lit 18th-century lodge room with a long wooden table, a row of sealed certificates and a map, and no people in view

storyboard.claim: Knigge builds a rigid hierarchy out of thin air over the network.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Empty lodge room where the invented structure sits.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains how the hierarchy is laid over the network.
storyboard.addedInformation: A new member no longer joins as a brother.

storyboard.claim: Members advance through four invented ranks.
storyboard.onScreenText: MANURVAL, MINOR ILLUMINATUS, SCOTTISH KNIGHT, MAGUS
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The rigid hierarchy shown as steps.
storyboard.addedInformation: Each rank is earned by proving yourself.

storyboard.claim: A pure flat network is mostly useless for wielding real power.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Generalises the Knigge case into a rule.
storyboard.addedInformation: Power needs more than shared ideas.

image.subject: a crowd of ordinary people in plain clothes gathered loosely in a cobbled town square at dusk, seen from behind, with no clear leader

storyboard.claim: Flat networks can share ideas and stage protests but cannot coordinate action.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Loose crowd in a square with no focal leader.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the strengths and limits of a flat network.
storyboard.addedInformation: A crowd without structure is good only for protest.

image.subject: an ordinary man of mid-thirties in plain clothes seen from behind, standing among gold-braided officials in a formal 18th-century hall

storyboard.claim: To conquer a hierarchy, a network must adopt its geometry.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Plain man among formal officials, showing disguise.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from flat failure to the strategy of disguise.
storyboard.addedInformation: The network copies its enemy's structure.

image.subject: a candle-lit 18th-century lodge room with a wooden table, books, a map and a row of chairs arranged for a formal meeting

storyboard.claim: The broader Freemason network was hijacked to build the Illuminati ranks.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The lodge room, the hijacked network's setting.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns to the Freemason network the Illuminati used.
storyboard.addedInformation: The lodge is the host network for the Illuminati.

storyboard.claim: Nineteenth-century lithographs show Washington proudly wearing his Masonic apron.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the Freemason appeal to elite men.
storyboard.addedInformation: Washington was a Freemason.

storyboard.claim: Washington rejected the British monarchy and walked away from being a king.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the Washington point into irony.
storyboard.addedInformation: He refused to become king in America.

storyboard.claim: Why did a horizontal fraternal network lure powerful men?
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Raises the question the next beats answer.
storyboard.addedInformation: The question names Washington and the Duke of Saxe-Gotha.

image.subject: a German duke in an embroidered court coat seated at a candle-lit lodge table among plain-clothed men, a ribbon catching the light

storyboard.claim: A duke joined the lodge for its secret status.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Ducal figure in court coat at a lodge table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the question with a concrete figure.
storyboard.addedInformation: The duke is powerful and elite.

storyboard.claim: The network offered exclusive hierarchical status.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the reason the powerful joined.
storyboard.addedInformation: The status was exclusive to members.

storyboard.claim: The lodge gave men a new ladder above the uninitiated masses.
storyboard.onScreenText: NEW LADDER, SECRET STATUS, ABOVE THE MASSES
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Expands the status reason into three parts.
storyboard.addedInformation: Men at the top of society wanted an extra tower.

image.subject: a well-dressed gentleman of mid-thirties seen from behind, standing in a candle-lit lodge room in front of a circle of plain-clothed men

storyboard.claim: Men at the top of society joined to feel they were at the top of a secret tower.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A gentleman in a lodge circle.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the men described in the prior beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: The network elevates its members.

image.subject: Adolph Knigge, a German baron in his thirties, well-fed, embroidered dark-green court coat, powdered hair, a lace jabot, standing apart from a plain-clothed shoemaker across a candle-lit table

storyboard.claim: Knigge understood that a duke would not sit as an equal with a shoemaker.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Baron and shoemaker kept apart at the table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Returns to Knigge with the ego point.
storyboard.addedInformation: The shoemaker is the everyday member.

storyboard.claim: Did Knigge ruin a beautiful flat network?
storyboard.relationToPrevious: A speaker challenges Knigge.
storyboard.addedInformation: The network was built on reason and equality.

storyboard.claim: Knigge cynically turned the flat network into an elite tower.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States the objection in full.
storyboard.addedInformation: Weishaupt's vision of no ranks was corrupted.

storyboard.claim: Without the fake hierarchy the aristocrats would never have joined.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the objection with history.
storyboard.addedInformation: The fake ranks drew the aristocratic members.

storyboard.claim: Would a flat network of radical students have died out?
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pushes the debate forward.
storyboard.addedInformation: The flat network was made of students.

image.subject: a group of young men in plain 1780s clothes drinking beer and arguing around a wooden table in a Bavarian tavern, mugs and a candle on the table

storyboard.claim: A flat student club would have drunk beer, complained and vanished.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Students in a tavern with beer and argument.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the concrete picture behind the claim.
storyboard.addedInformation: Complaints about the church would not sustain the group.

storyboard.claim: The structure turned a drinking club into a weapon.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Concludes the structure argument.
storyboard.addedInformation: Fake ranks, mysteries and initiations did the work.

image.subject: a late-18th-century Bavarian university professor in his late twenties, slim, powdered-hair style, dark frock coat with a white cravat, walking into a formal palace hall to meet state officials

storyboard.claim: The Illuminati could interface directly with state power structures.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the hierarchy disguise working on the state.
storyboard.addedInformation: Weishaupt was the professor who founded the lodge.

storyboard.claim: To destroy the tower, the square has to disguise itself as a tower.
storyboard.onScreenText: THE SQUARE DISGUISED AS A TOWER
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sums up the paradox just described.
storyboard.addedInformation: This is the central paradox of the chapter.

storyboard.claim: The shadow hierarchy gained the attention of the real one and let the Illuminati punch above their weight.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why the paradox worked.
storyboard.addedInformation: The shadow tower gained real attention.

image.subject: a Bavarian official's letter with a red wax seal lying on a wooden desk beside an open ledger, a candle burning down

storyboard.claim: Bavarian authorities found out, panicked and outlawed the Illuminati in 1784.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Official letter with seal on a desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Ends the Illuminati stretch with the state's response.
storyboard.addedInformation: The authorities acted by decree.

storyboard.claim: The square must interface with the tower to achieve true power.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Generalises the pattern and leads to the next case.
storyboard.addedInformation: The most successful network in modern history comes next.

image.subject: a gilded 19th-century hall in Vienna where emperors, kings and diplomats in gold braid and medals stand around a large table after the Napoleonic wars

storyboard.claim: The Congress of Vienna in 1815 ended the Napoleonic Wars.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gilded hall with diplomats around a table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the next case study.
storyboard.addedInformation: The wars had lasted decades.

image.subject: an opulent 19th-century room of emperors and kings covered in gold braid and medals, gathered around a giant sweeping map of Europe

storyboard.claim: The room of Vienna is opulent and filled with gold and braid.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Crowded gilded room with the map in view.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets the scene described in beat 151.
storyboard.addedInformation: Emperors, kings and diplomats are all present.

image.subject: a diplomat in a gold-braided coat leaning over a large map of Europe, drawing a line across it with a pen

storyboard.claim: Diplomats casually redraw borders and trade millions of lives.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A diplomat drawing a border line.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the action in the room.
storyboard.addedInformation: The redrawing traded lives.

storyboard.claim: The Congress was called the cake of kings, the top-down power of monarchy.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the room's power.
storyboard.addedInformation: The phrase is the historians' own label.

storyboard.claim: Simultaneously, a different kind of power operates just outside the room.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns from the official room to the counting house.
storyboard.addedInformation: The different power is horizontal.

image.subject: Mayer Amschel Rothschild, an 18th-century Frankfurt merchant-banker in his fifties, stout, dark wool coat, round spectacles, ledger in hand, standing in the doorway of a busy counting house

storyboard.claim: A frantic Rothschild counting house operates just outside the official room.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Rothschild in a counting house doorway with a ledger.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the Rothschild network.
storyboard.addedInformation: The counting house is busy and frantic.

image.subject: an ordinary courier in a mud-spattered riding coat hurrying out of a doorway, a leather pouch of sealed letters under his arm

storyboard.claim: Couriers move information and money faster than any king's army can march.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Courier with a letter pouch hurrying from a door.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the couriers the previous beat named.
storyboard.addedInformation: Money moves faster than armies.

storyboard.claim: The Rothschilds ran a decentralised family network with brothers in several cities.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the family members in the network.
storyboard.addedInformation: Nathan in London, James in Paris, Solomon in Vienna, Carl in Naples, Amsel in Frankfurt.

image.subject: a long wooden counting-house table with five sealed letters laid out in a row, each addressed to a different European capital, a brass scale beside them

storyboard.claim: Five brothers in five cities form five nodes constantly communicating.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Five letters in a row on a table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the family names into a visible network.
storyboard.addedInformation: The letters show constant communication.
